chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from al-Ahwasi, from al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn al-Lu'lu'i, from Ibn Sinan, from Hudhayfah ibn Mansur, who said: He said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

about a man who carries goods for a wage; if the goods are lost, and he is pleased/content to compensate their owners, do they take (the compensation) from him? He said to me: 'He is an amanah (trustworthy carrier).' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then they do not take anything from him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a carrier who loses goods and is content to compensate the owner?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a carrier deemed 'amin' (trustworthy/good faith) who loses entrusted goods is not liable for damages unless he is proven negligent or breaches specific terms, reflecting the Shia legal principle that liability arises from fault rather than mere loss. This ruling underscores the importance of intent and status in commercial contracts, distinguishing between a simple custodian and a guarantor. It highlights the juristic preference for leniency in cases of good-faith custodianship, a key concept in Shia fiqh of transactions.
